definition: A no-par stock refers to stock that does not have a minimum or face value, while par value stock does have a minimum value set out in the corporate charter of the issuing company. In general, the par value of a stock has little relation to market value. Most corporations that set a par value for their stock do so at a nominal amount. For instance, the par value of Apple stock is set at $0.00001 per share, likewise most other companies set the par value anywhere from $0.00001 to $0.01. Notably, this is not the case for the par values set for bonds, these par values represent the amount the issuer promises to pay the bondholder upon the bond's maturity. Therefore, stocks are uniquely able to have no par value. No-par stock gives the corporation's board discretion to decide the face value of the stock in lieu of a par value. This gives the board flexibility in determining the amount of stated capital (the portion of a company's equity that they can not distribute and must retain to protect creditors) or surplus capital (capital in excess of the stated capital) and dividend distributions. The majority of states, including those who have adopted the Model Business Corporation Act (MBCA), have removed the distinction between par/no-par stocks. Instead opting for an approach that bases distributions on a corporation's solvency.
